title: GitHub Quiz
description: Revisit the key ideas in GitHub. Read each choice carefully. You can try the quiz again after reviewing the lessons.

questions.question: Does a local commit automatically upload to GitHub?
questions.explanation: Git records file history on a computer. GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds pages for collaboration. You can learn local Git without a GitHub account. The local and hosted copies are separate places. A local commit does not upload itself to GitHub.

questions.question: Where do proposed code changes appear?
questions.explanation: A GitHub repository page has areas for code and collaboration. Start with its README, then inspect the files and recent changes. Each area answers a different question. To understand what a project does, the README is usually the best starting point.

questions.question: What happens before merging in this flow?
questions.explanation: GitHub Flow is a lightweight way to work on changes. A focused branch and pull request let people inspect an idea before it joins the main branch. The change has a review stage between writing code and combining it with main. Exact project rules decide who may merge.

questions.question: Which detail helps reproduce the bug?
options: Only a request to fix everything
questions.explanation: A GitHub issue can record a bug or proposed task. A useful bug report gives steps, expected behaviour and actual behaviour. A maintainer can repeat the exact steps. The issue describes a problem; it does not itself change the search code.

questions.question: Which branch receives the proposed change?
questions.explanation: A pull request, often called a PR, proposes combining changes from one branch into another. Its description should explain the result for a reviewer. The base receives the proposed changes. The head holds the change being reviewed. The explanation links the edit to a visible behaviour.

questions.question: What does this change handle?
questions.explanation: The Files changed view shows the difference a PR proposes. Review the actual lines and ask focused questions about behaviour and edge cases. The edit ignores letter case, but it does not trim spaces. The review question identifies another case that needs a decision.

questions.question: Which outcome says work is needed before approval?
questions.explanation: A GitHub review may comment, approve or request changes. Project branch rules determine which reviews are required before merging. The outcomes communicate different levels of readiness. A review approval is evidence from a person, not a guarantee that every bug is absent.

questions.question: What does a passing check prove?
options: Its configured checks passed in that run
questions.explanation: GitHub Actions can run a workflow when code changes. A workflow is a configured set of jobs and steps. Its check reports whether those steps succeeded. The green result says the configured test command passed in that run. It does not prove the workflow checked every browser or every page.

questions.question: Why require a status check before merging?
options: To enforce an agreed automated check
questions.explanation: Repository rules can require reviews or status checks before a branch accepts changes. This helps a team apply the same process consistently. The plan records a review process. Available settings depend on the repository and GitHub plan; no rule is changed by reading this lesson.

questions.question: Which copy is on the local computer?
questions.explanation: A fork is a hosted repository linked to an upstream project. A clone is a local repository copy. A fork can hold proposed contributions without granting write access to upstream. The fork lives on GitHub and the clone lives on a computer. Moving commits between them requires separate Git operations.

questions.question: What does the release note explain?
questions.explanation: A Git tag names a specific point in history. A GitHub release can add notes and downloadable files around a tag. The notes tell users what changed and what still matters. Later commits are not automatically part of the tagged version.

questions.question: Where do you first check reuse conditions?
questions.explanation: Community files help people use and contribute to a repository. A licence explains reuse conditions; other files describe participation and reporting. These files answer different questions. Read the security reporting instructions before posting sensitive vulnerability details publicly.
